claim: The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted HPV vaccination programmes worldwide.
source: The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted HPV vaccination programmes worldwide.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations to WHO and other sources documenting the disruption.

claim: Shifting from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination strategy under 60% coverage would increase resilience by 2.8-fold from 107 to 302 cases per 100,000 girls born in the case of 5-year disruption with no coverage.
source: In the base case of 5-year disruption with no coverage, shifting from GO to GN strategy under 60% coverage (before disruption) would increase the resilience, in terms of cervical cancer cases still prevented in the disrupted birth cohorts per 100,000 girls born, by 2.8-fold from 107 to 302 cases
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model-based analysis presented in the manuscript, with specific numerical results.

claim: Shifting from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination strategy under 90% coverage would increase resilience by 2.2-fold from 209 to 464 cases per 100,000 girls born in the case of 5-year disruption with no coverage.
source: In the base case of 5-year disruption with no coverage, shifting from GO to GN strategy under 60% coverage (before disruption) would increase the resilience, in terms of cervical cancer cases still prevented in the disrupted birth cohorts per 100,000 girls born, by 2.8-fold from 107 to 302 cases, and by 2.2-fold from 209 to 464 cases under 90% coverage.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the model-based analysis with specific numerical results.

claim: Under girls-only vaccination with 60% coverage, the age-standardised incidence rate of cervical cancer in India in the long term decreased from 11.0 to 4.7 cases per 100,000 woman-years, which is above the WHO elimination threshold.
source: Under GO vaccination with 60% coverage, the age-standardised incidence rate of cervical cancer in India in the long term with vaccination decreased from 11.0 to 4.7 cases per 100,000 woman-years (above threshold)
evidence: This is a model-based estimate comparing the incidence rate to the WHO threshold.

claim: Under gender-neutral vaccination with 60% coverage, the age-standardised incidence rate of cervical cancer in India in the long term decreased to 2.8 cases per 100,000 woman-years, which is below the WHO elimination threshold.
source: as compared to 2.8 cases (below threshold) under GN with 60% coverage
evidence: This is a model-based estimate comparing the incidence rate to the WHO threshold.

claim: Under gender-neutral vaccination with 90% coverage, the age-standardised incidence rate of cervical cancer in India in the long term decreased to 2.4 cases per 100,000 woman-years, which is below the WHO elimination threshold.
source: 2.4 cases (below threshold) under GN with 90% coverage
evidence: This is a model-based estimate comparing the incidence rate to the WHO threshold.

claim: The World Health Assembly adopted the Global Strategy for cervical cancer elimination in August 2020.
source: In August 2020, the World Health Assembly adopted the Global Strategy for cervical cancer elimination, with the overarching target of reducing the age-standardised incidence rate (ASIR) of cervical cancer to fewer than 4 cases per 100,000 woman-years (WHO, 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO 2020a.

claim: The WHO elimination threshold for cervical cancer is fewer than 4 cases per 100,000 woman-years.
source: with the overarching target of reducing the age-standardised incidence rate (ASIR) of cervical cancer to fewer than 4 cases per 100,000 woman-years (WHO, 2020a)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO 2020a.

claim: The WHO recommends fully vaccinating 90% of all girls with the HPV vaccine by age 15 years to reach the cervical cancer elimination target.
source: To reach this target, the following actions have been recommended: to fully vaccinate 90% of all girls with the HPV vaccine by age 15 years, to screen 70% of women using a high-performance test by the age of 35, and again by the age of 45, and to treat 90% of women with pre-cancer and 90% of women with invasive cancer (WHO, 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO 2020b.

claim: The WHO recommends screening 70% of women using a high-performance test by the age of 35, and again by the age of 45 to reach the cervical cancer elimination target.
source: to screen 70% of women using a high-performance test by the age of 35, and again by the age of 45
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO 2020b.

claim: The WHO recommends treating 90% of women with pre-cancer and 90% of women with invasive cancer to reach the cervical cancer elimination target.
source: to treat 90% of women with pre-cancer and 90% of women with invasive cancer (WHO, 2020b)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO 2020b.

claim: HPV vaccination worldwide was affected by the COVID-19 pandemic through slowed down or interrupted vaccine delivery in countries with active programmes.
source: More specifically, HPV vaccination worldwide was affected at many different levels: (a) where population-based HPV vaccination programmes were already active, vaccine delivery slowed down or was interrupted (Muhoza et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Muhoza et al., 2021.

claim: The launch of HPV vaccination programmes was delayed in several countries, particularly in resource-limited settings, due to the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: (b) the launch of HPV vaccination programmes was delayed in several countries, in particular in resource-limited settings (The Lancet Oncology, 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to The Lancet Oncology, 2022.

claim: The production of HPV vaccines was limited in favour of manufacturing other vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: (c) the production of HPV vaccines was also limited in favour of manufacturing other vaccines (WHO, 2022a)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO, 2022a.

claim: Health-care systems or public-health programmes at a local level have regularly suffered severe disruption caused by factors such as changes in political commitment, financial constraints, scepticism of the civil society, geo-political unrest, and environmental disasters.
source: health-care systems or public-health programmes at a local level have also regularly suffered severe disruption caused by other factors such as changes in political commitment, financial constraints, scepticism of the civil society, geo-political unrest, and environmental disasters (Colón-López et al., 2021; Gallagher et al., 2017; Germani et al., 2022; Jawad et al., 2021; Larson, 2020; McGrath, 2022)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Disruptions to organised disease prevention and control programmes may multiply public health crises.
source: These partial or complete disruptions to organised disease prevention and control programmes may multiply public health crises (Sharpless, 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sharpless, 2020.

claim: Disruptions to organised disease prevention and control programmes may provoke substantial, usually unquantified waste of human, logistic, and financial resources.
source: as well as provoke substantial, usually unquantified waste of human, logistic, and financial resources (Richards et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Richards et al., 2020.

claim: A previous study conducted before the COVID-19 pandemic in a high-income country showed that the addition of vaccination in boys to a programme targeting girls only could increase the resilience of the vaccination programme.
source: In a previous study, conducted before the COVID-19 pandemic in a high-income country, we showed that the addition of vaccination in boys to a programme targeting girls only could increase the resilience of the vaccination programme (Elfström et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Elfström et al., 2016.

claim: India is currently the country with the largest burden of cervical cancer.
source: Currently, India is the country with the largest burden of cervical cancer (Bonjour et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bonjour et al., 2021.

claim: Cervical cancer screening is still limitedly accessible in India, with less than 3% ever-in-life coverage in women aged 30–49 years.
source: Cervical cancer screening is still limitedly accessible in India, with less than 3% ever-in-life coverage in women aged 30–49 years (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2019; The Lancet Oncology, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sankaranarayanan et al., 2019 and The Lancet Oncology, 2022.

claim: HPV vaccination (in girls) has been introduced in two Indian states with high vaccination coverage.
source: HPV vaccination (in girls) has been introduced in two Indian states with high vaccination coverage (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sankaranarayanan et al., 2019.

claim: Marketing authorisation has been granted to an indigenous HPV vaccine in India.
source: Following the recent marketing authorisation granted to an indigenous vaccine (The Lancet Oncology, 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to The Lancet Oncology, 2022.

claim: The prospect of introducing HPV vaccination into the national immunisation programme in India has significantly improved following the marketing authorisation of an indigenous vaccine.
source: Following the recent marketing authorisation granted to an indigenous vaccine (The Lancet Oncology, 2022), the prospect of introducing HPV vaccination into the national immunisation programme has also significantly improved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the marketing authorisation, supported by citation.

claim: Life-time cervical cancer cases prevented in the birth cohorts vaccinated prior to the disruption period ranged between 562 and 807 cases per 100,000 girls born in the four highlighted scenarios.
source: Life-time cervical cancer cases prevented in the birth cohorts vaccinated prior to the disruption period ranged between 562 (UI: 444, 676) and 807 (UI: 752, 853) cases per 100,000 girls born in the four highlighted scenarios.
evidence: This is a model-based estimate with uncertainty intervals.

claim: The highest impact in undisrupted cohorts was achieved by the gender-neutral strategy with 90% coverage.
source: The highest impact was achieved by the GN strategy with 90% coverage, closely followed by GO with 90% coverage, then GN with 60% coverage, and then GO with 60% coverage (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on model results shown in Figure 1.

claim: The girls-only strategy with 60% coverage had the lowest resilience among the four highlighted scenarios.
source: Among the four highlighted scenarios, the GO strategy with 60% coverage also had the lowest resilience
evidence: This is based on model results comparing resilience across scenarios.

claim: Under girls-only vaccination with 60% coverage, the life-time number of cervical cancer cases prevented would drop from 562 cases in undisrupted cohorts to 107 cases per 100,000 girls born in disrupted cohorts.
source: We found that the life-time number of cervical cancer cases prevented would drop considerably from 562 (UI: 444, 676) cases in the undisrupted cohorts to 107 (UI: 7, 214) cases per 100,000 girls born in the disrupted cohorts (i.e., resilience of 107).
evidence: This is a model-based estimate with uncertainty intervals.

claim: Increasing coverage under the girls-only strategy from 60% to 90% would lead to a small absolute gain in resilience from 107 to 209 cases prevented per 100,000 girls born.
source: Increasing the coverage under the GO strategy from 60% to 90% would lead to a small absolute gain in resilience, from 107 (UI: 7, 214) to 209 (UI: 81, 340) cases prevented per 100,000 girls born
evidence: This is a model-based estimate with uncertainty intervals.

claim: Switching from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination under 60% coverage led to a moderate gain of impact in undisrupted cohorts from 562 to 647 cases prevented per 100,000 girls born.
source: By contrast, switching from GO to GN vaccination, under 60% coverage, led to a moderate gain of impact in the undisrupted cohorts from 562 (UI: 444, 676) to 647 (UI: 539, 746) cases prevented
evidence: This is a model-based estimate with uncertainty intervals.

claim: Switching from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination under 60% coverage led to a substantial increase in resilience from 107 to 302 cases prevented per 100,000 girls born.
source: but a substantial increase in resilience from 107 (UI: 7, 214) to 302 (UI: 170, 437) cases prevented per 100,000 girls born
evidence: This is a model-based estimate with uncertainty intervals.

claim: Gender-neutral vaccination with 90% coverage led to the highest impact of 807 cases prevented per 100,000 girls born in undisrupted cohorts.
source: Finally, GN vaccination with 90% coverage led to the highest impact of 807 (UI: 752, 853) cases prevented per 100,000 girls born in the undisrupted cohorts
evidence: This is a model-based estimate with uncertainty intervals.

claim: Gender-neutral vaccination with 90% coverage led to the highest resilience of 464 cases prevented per 100,000 girls born in disrupted cohorts.
source: as well as the highest resilience of 464 (UI: 328, 602) cases prevented per 100,000 girls born in the disrupted cohorts
evidence: This is a model-based estimate with uncertainty intervals.

claim: There is a trade-off between dose-efficiency and resilience when comparing girls-only and gender-neutral vaccination strategies.
source: Considering the required number of vaccine doses, we found a trade-off between dose-efficiency and resilience. In general, GO vaccination favoured dose-efficiency and GN vaccination favoured resilience (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference from model results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Girls-only vaccination favours dose-efficiency while gender-neutral vaccination favours resilience.
source: In general, GO vaccination favoured dose-efficiency and GN vaccination favoured resilience (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference from model results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Switching from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination under 60% coverage would yield a higher gain in resilience (2.8-fold) than increasing girls-only coverage from 60% to 90% (2-fold).
source: However, this switch from GO to GN vaccination would yield a higher gain in resilience than when increasing GO coverage from 60% to 90% (2.8-fold versus 2-fold increase).
evidence: This is based on model results comparing resilience ratios.

claim: Switching from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination under 90% coverage would require an additional doubling of the number of doses.
source: Similarly, switching from GO to GN vaccination under 90% coverage would require an additional doubling of the number of doses
evidence: This is a logical inference based on vaccinating both boys and girls instead of girls only.

claim: Switching from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination under 90% coverage would only marginally improve the impact in undisrupted cohorts but would produce a 2.2-fold gain in resilience.
source: and only marginally improve the impact in the undisrupted cohorts, but would produce a 2.2-fold gain in resilience
evidence: This is based on model results comparing impact and resilience.

claim: In states with high cervical cancer incidence, there is slightly lower resilience under the girls-only strategy and a slightly greater relative gain in resilience when switching from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination than in states with low incidence.
source: Interestingly, in the states with high cervical cancer incidence, we found slightly lower resilience under the GO strategy and a slightly greater relative gain in resilience when switching from GO to GN vaccination than in states with low incidence (Supplementary file 3, Appendix 2—figures 1–3).
evidence: This is based on model results stratified by state-specific incidence.

claim: In the base case, the resilience ratio for switching from girls-only to gender-neutral strategy under 60% coverage was 3-fold in states with high cervical cancer incidence and 2.7-fold in states with low cervical cancer incidence.
source: In the base case, for example, the resilience ratio for switching from GO to GN strategy (under 60% coverage) was 3-fold in states with high cervical cancer incidence and 2.7-fold in states with low cervical cancer incidence.
evidence: This is based on model results stratified by state-specific incidence.

claim: Sensitivity analyses on less strong disruption in vaccination coverage or alternative durations of disruption yielded higher resilience with gender-neutral than girls-only vaccination.
source: Sensitivity analyses on less strong disruption in vaccination coverage or alternative durations of disruption also yielded higher resilience with GN than GO vaccination (Table 1, Appendix 2—figures 2–3).
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analyses presented in Table 1 and figures.

claim: The gain in resilience by switching from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination was most evident under complete disruption of vaccination (0% coverage at disruption) but still consistently found under less strong disruption (20% or 40% coverage at disruption).
source: The gain in resilience by switching from GO to GN vaccination was most evident under complete disruption of vaccination (i.e., 0% coverage at disruption) but still consistently found under less strong disruption (i.e., 20% or 40% coverage at disruption) (Table 1 part II, Appendix 2—figure 2).
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analyses presented in Table 1 and figures.

claim: Resilience decreased with longer duration of disruption, with any vaccination strategy, but was always higher with the gender-neutral strategy.
source: As expected, resilience decreased with longer duration of disruption, with any vaccination strategy, but was always higher with the GN strategy (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on model results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The gain in resilience by switching from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination was consistently above 2.7-fold under 60% coverage and above 2.0-fold under 90% coverage across different durations of disruption.
source: The gain in resilience by switching from GO to GN vaccination was consistently above 2.7-fold under 60% coverage and above 2.0-fold under 90% coverage (Table 1 part III).
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analyses presented in Table 1.

claim: In the scenario with no restart of vaccination, gender-neutral vaccination could ensure some resilience of at least 125 cases prevented per 100,000 girls born for eight birth cohorts from the start of disruption.
source: Finally, in the scenario with no restart of vaccination, GN vaccination could ensure some resilience of at least 125 cases prevented per 100,000 girls born for eight birth cohorts from the start of disruption (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on model results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Introducing girls-only vaccination with 60% coverage would reduce the nationwide age-standardised incidence rate of cervical cancer from 11 cases to 4.7 cases per 100,000 woman-years in 100 years, which remains above the WHO elimination threshold.
source: Introducing GO vaccination with 60% coverage would have the lowest impact, reducing the nationwide ASIR of cervical cancer from 11 cases, which is the present level before the introduction of vaccination, to 4.7 (UI: 4.3, 5.1) cases per 100,000 woman-years in 100 years, but this remained above the WHO elimination threshold (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a model-based estimate shown in Figure 3.

claim: The other highlighted scenarios (girls-only 90%, gender-neutral 60%, gender-neutral 90%) enabled elimination to be reached within 55–62 years.
source: The other highlighted scenarios enabled elimination to be reached within 55–62 years.
evidence: This is based on model results.

claim: Introducing gender-neutral vaccination with 60% coverage in both girls and boys would reduce incidence down to 2.8 cases per 100,000 woman-years, below the elimination threshold.
source: Introducing GN vaccination with 60% coverage in both girls and boys would reduce incidence down to 2.8 (UI: 2.5, 3.2) cases per 100,000 woman-years, hence below the elimination threshold.
evidence: This is a model-based estimate with uncertainty intervals.

claim: The girls-only strategy with 90% coverage, as recommended by WHO, would decrease incidence below the threshold to 2.4 cases per 100,000 woman-years.
source: The GO strategy with 90% coverage, as recommended by WHO, would also decrease incidence below the threshold to 2.4 (UI: 2.3, 2.6) cases per 100,000 woman-years.
evidence: This is a model-based estimate with uncertainty intervals.

claim: Given the already high vaccination coverage of 90% in girls, switching to the gender-neutral strategy would only marginally reduce incidence to 2.3 cases per 100,000 woman-years.
source: Lastly, given the already high vaccination coverage of 90% in girls, switching to the GN strategy would only marginally reduce incidence to 2.3 (UI: 2.2, 2.3) cases per 100,000 woman-years.
evidence: This is a model-based estimate with uncertainty intervals.

claim: Without vaccination in boys, the WHO elimination threshold could be reached through a critical girls-only coverage of 70%.
source: Without vaccination in boys, the WHO elimination threshold could be reached through a critical GO coverage of 70% (UI: 65, 73) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a model-based estimate shown in Figure 4.

claim: With vaccination in boys, a lower critical coverage in girls might be sufficient for elimination.
source: With vaccination in boys, a lower critical coverage in girls might be sufficient for elimination.
evidence: This is an inference from model results.

claim: Coverage between 50% and 70% in girls might be sufficient for elimination when combined with moderate coverage (30%) in boys.
source: For instance, coverage between 50% and 70% in girls might also be sufficient for elimination when combined with moderate coverage (30%) in boys (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on model results shown in Figure 4.

claim: Disruption of vaccination does not prevent countries from reaching the elimination threshold eventually, provided vaccination resumes after disruption.
source: Finally, while disruption of vaccination does not prevent countries from reaching the elimination threshold eventually (provided vaccination resumes after disruption), it can prolong the number of years taken to attain this goal (Appendix 2—figure 4).
evidence: This is based on model results shown in Appendix 2—figure 4.

claim: Disruption of vaccination can prolong the number of years taken to reach the elimination threshold.
source: it can prolong the number of years taken to attain this goal (Appendix 2—figure 4)
evidence: This is based on model results shown in Appendix 2—figure 4.

claim: Under the girls-only strategy with 90% coverage, disruption of vaccination for 5 years would delay reaching elimination from 57 to 65 years since the start of vaccination.
source: Under the GO strategy with 90% coverage, for instance, disruption of vaccination for 5 years (as in the base case) would delay reaching elimination from 57 to 65 years since the start of vaccination.
evidence: This is a model-based estimate.

claim: By switching to gender-neutral strategy under 90% coverage, elimination could be reached in 58 years since the start of vaccination, even with disruption.
source: By switching to GN strategy (under 90% coverage), elimination could be reached in 58 years since the start of vaccination, even with disruption.
evidence: This is a model-based estimate.

claim: The age difference between sexual partners is an important determinant underlying the gain in resilience by switching from girls-only to gender-neutral vaccination.
source: An important determinant underlying the gain in resilience by switching from GO to GN vaccination is likely the age difference between sexual partners.
evidence: This is an inference from the model results and understanding of transmission dynamics.

claim: Men are on average older than women within sexual partnerships almost everywhere worldwide.
source: In general, men are on average older than women within sexual partnerships almost everywhere worldwide (Wellings et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wellings et al., 2006.

claim: In cases of vaccination disruption, the birth cohorts of boys vaccinated before the disruption would indirectly protect the cohorts of younger girls who missed out on vaccination during the disruption period.
source: In cases of vaccination disruption, the birth cohorts of boys vaccinated before the disruption would indirectly protect the cohorts of younger girls who missed out on vaccination during the disruption period.
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of herd immunity and age-mixing patterns.

claim: The magnitude of the resilience attributable to gender-neutral HPV vaccination is expected to be different across populations due to population-specific social norms regulating sexual behaviour.
source: Since sexual behaviour is regulated by population-specific social norms, the magnitude of the resilience attributable to GN HPV vaccination is also expected to be different across populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between sexual behaviour and transmission dynamics.

claim: In India, the age difference between male and female partners is on average 7 years.
source: In India, for example, the age difference between male and female partners is on average 7 years (USAID, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to USAID, 2017.

claim: The average age difference between partners in India (7 years) is similar to the number of birth cohorts still retaining some protection by gender-neutral vaccination when no restart of vaccination after disruption was simulated.
source: similar to the number of birth cohorts still retaining some protection by GN vaccination when we simulated no restart of vaccination after disruption
evidence: This is an inference connecting the age difference data to model results.

claim: Vaccinating boys is a more direct way to reduce the force of infection in men than vaccinating girls.
source: However, vaccinating boys is a more direct way to reduce the force of infection in men than vaccinating girls, which is the likely mechanism underlying the higher resilience achieved by GN strategy than GO strategy.
evidence: This is an inference based on understanding of transmission dynamics.

claim: Elimination across India could be reached with a critical level of girls-only coverage of 70%, which falls between the average coverage observed among girls aged 9–15 years living in countries with an active HPV vaccination programme (53%) and the coverage recommended by the WHO (90%).
source: In principle, elimination across India could be reached with a critical level of GO coverage of 70%, which falls between the average coverage observed among girls aged 9–15 years living in countries with an active HPV vaccination programme, that is, 53% (Bruni et al., 2021), and the coverage recommended by the WHO, that is, 90% (WHO, 2020b).
evidence: This is based on model results and citations to observed coverage and WHO recommendations.

claim: The average coverage observed among girls aged 9–15 years living in countries with an active HPV vaccination programme is 53%.
source: the average coverage observed among girls aged 9–15 years living in countries with an active HPV vaccination programme, that is, 53% (Bruni et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bruni et al., 2021.

claim: Cervical cancer elimination could be reached with 50–70% coverage in girls when combined with moderate coverage in boys, even if coverage in boys were lower than that of girls.
source: On the other hand, our model-based estimates suggest that cervical cancer elimination could be reached with 50–70% coverage in girls when combined with moderate coverage in boys, even if coverage in boys were lower than that of girls.
evidence: This is based on model results.

claim: In cases where girls-only coverage is already above 70%, gender-neutral vaccination would allow even more ambitious cervical cancer control targets to be reached.
source: In cases where GO coverage is already above 70%, GN vaccination would allow even more ambitious cervical cancer control targets to be reached
evidence: This is an inference from model results.

claim: Gender-neutral vaccination might eventually make cervical screening targeted to vaccinated birth cohorts redundant.
source: which might eventually make cervical screening targeted to vaccinated birth cohorts redundant (Tota et al., 2020)
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Tota et al., 2020.

claim: Reaching elimination might be challenging in the Indian states with the highest baseline cervical cancer incidence before vaccination.
source: Moreover, as previously reported (Man et al., 2022), reaching elimination might be challenging in the Indian states with the highest baseline cervical cancer incidence before vaccination.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Man et al., 2022.

claim: In Indian states with the highest baseline cervical cancer incidence, additional measures such as gender-neutral vaccination would be even more relevant.
source: In these cases, additional measures such as GN vaccination would be even more relevant.
evidence: This is an inference from the previous claim about challenges in high-incidence states.

claim: The critical levels of HPV vaccination coverage found for India are not necessarily generalisable to other populations.
source: A limitation of this study is that the critical levels of HPV vaccination coverage found for India are not necessarily generalisable to other populations.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: Baseline cervical cancer incidence and the magnitude of herd effect should be considered when determining critical levels of HPV vaccination coverage.
source: Baseline cervical cancer incidence and the magnitude of herd effect, that is, the indirect protection offered by the vaccinated to the unvaccinated individuals of a population against HPV infection (Malagón et al., 2018) should be considered.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Malagón et al., 2018.

claim: Herd effect is the indirect protection offered by the vaccinated to the unvaccinated individuals of a population against HPV infection.
source: the magnitude of herd effect, that is, the indirect protection offered by the vaccinated to the unvaccinated individuals of a population against HPV infection (Malagón et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to Malagón et al., 2018.

claim: Baseline cervical cancer incidence and herd effect are governed by local sexual behaviour.
source: These are, in turn, governed by local sexual behaviour (Bosch et al., 1994; Schulte-Frohlinde et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bosch et al., 1994 and Schulte-Frohlinde et al., 2022.

claim: The critical level of vaccination coverage to reach cervical cancer elimination is context-specific.
source: As mentioned above for resilience, the critical level of vaccination coverage to reach cervical cancer elimination will be context-specific (Baussano et al., 2018; Lehtinen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baussano et al., 2018 and Lehtinen et al., 2022.

claim: Extrapolation of the results of this study to other populations will be limited to those sharing similar patterns of demography, social norms, and cervical cancer epidemiology as India.
source: Extrapolation of the results of this study to other populations will be limited to those sharing similar patterns of demography, social norms, and cervical cancer epidemiology as India.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: The principle of improving the resilience of cervical cancer prevention through a shift to gender-neutral vaccination is expected to be widely applicable.
source: Nevertheless, we expect the principle of improving the resilience of cervical cancer prevention through a shift to GN vaccination to be widely applicable
evidence: This is speculation based on the consistency of results.

claim: The consistency of results in India when stratifying by state-specific cervical cancer incidence supports the wide applicability of the principle of improving resilience through gender-neutral vaccination.
source: and this is supported by the consistency of our results in India when stratifying by state-specific cervical cancer incidence
evidence: This is based on model results stratified by state.

claim: The study did not explore changes in sexual behaviour in the population due to disruption.
source: For example, we did not explore changes in sexual behaviour in the population due to disruption, which occurs in dire circumstances like a pandemic.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: The study accounted for a large variation in the duration of disruption and in vaccination coverage at disruption through sensitivity analyses.
source: However, we did account for a large variation in the duration of disruption and in vaccination coverage at disruption through our sensitivity analyses.
evidence: This describes the methods used in the study.

claim: The study did not consider the influence of choice of HPV vaccine.
source: In addition, we did not consider the influence of choice of HPV vaccine
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: A quadrivalent vaccine would be the likely choice for India due to the price advantage.
source: as a quadrivalent vaccine (either indigenously produced or Gardasil) would be the likely choice for India due to the price advantage
evidence: This is speculation based on economic considerations.

claim: In cases of using a nonavalent vaccine, or a vaccine with higher levels of cross-protection, similar qualitative results for resilience are expected, and elimination of cervical cancer could be expected to be more easily achieved.
source: In cases of using a nonavalent vaccine, or a vaccine with higher levels of cross-protection, we expect similar qualitative results for resilience, and elimination of cervical cancer could be expected to be more easily achieved.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative vaccine scenarios.

claim: The study did not consider changes in cervical cancer screening.
source: We also did not consider changes in cervical cancer screening, as it is difficult to predict how much coverage of cervical cancer screening will increase in India in the coming years.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the study.

claim: Adding vaccination of boys to the routine coverage of girls would approximately double the required number of vaccine doses.
source: clearly adding vaccination of boys to the routine coverage of girls would approximately double the required number of vaccine doses
evidence: This is a logical inference based on vaccinating both sexes.

claim: Adding vaccination of boys to the routine coverage of girls would increase the financial effort to be made by the national government.
source: and would increase the financial effort to be made by the national government
evidence: This is a logical inference based on increased vaccine doses needed.

claim: Gender-neutral HPV vaccination schedules are economically attractive in high-income tender-based settings, particularly where girls-only vaccine uptake is below 80%.
source: It has been demonstrated that GN HPV vaccination schedules are economically attractive in high-income tender-based settings, in particular where GO vaccine uptake is below 80% (Qendri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Qendri et al., 2020.

claim: Gender-neutral vaccination is likely to be even more attractive in India where population-based screening programmes have not yet been widely implemented.
source: GN vaccination is likely to be even more attractive in India where population-based screening programmes have not yet been widely implemented.
evidence: This is speculation based on the lack of screening infrastructure.

claim: Extending vaccination to boys could be easier to put in place than improving coverage in girls from 60% to 90% in some contexts.
source: However, extending vaccination to boys could be easier to put in place than improving coverage in girls from 60% to 90% in some contexts.
evidence: This is speculation about implementation feasibility.

claim: Shifting from a two-dose to a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule could improve the affordability of gender-neutral vaccination.
source: Finally, shifting from a two-dose to a single-dose HPV vaccination schedule could also improve the affordability of GN vaccination.
evidence: This is speculation about cost reduction strategies.

claim: More research is needed to investigate the cost-effectiveness and affordability of gender-neutral vaccination in low-resource settings.
source: More research is needed to investigate the cost-effectiveness and affordability of GN vaccination in low-resource settings and how resilience should be accounted for in deciding the vaccination strategy.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: In high-income countries, most vaccination programmes were initiated with the girls-only strategy, often combined with catch-up in girls/women, and are now increasingly shifting towards gender-neutral vaccination.
source: In high-income countries, where affordability was less of an issue, most vaccination programmes were initiated with the GO strategy, often combined with catch-up in girls/women, and are now increasingly shifting towards GN vaccination.
evidence: This is a statement about observed trends in high-income countries.

claim: In resource-limited settings, once routine vaccination in girls has been implemented, countries may need to make a choice between boys' vaccination or female catch-up vaccination.
source: In resource-limited settings, once routine vaccination in girls has been implemented, countries may need to make a choice between boys' vaccination or female catch-up vaccination.
evidence: This is speculation about decision-making in resource-limited settings.

claim: The limited global vaccine supply will likely remain an important factor influencing decision-making on vaccination strategy in the coming years.
source: The limited global vaccine supply will likely remain an important factor influencing this decision-making process in the coming years (WHO, 2022b).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to WHO, 2022b.

claim: The choice of vaccination strategy at the country level should account for health-economic objectives, the type of health infrastructure already in place, and socio-cultural context.
source: In addition, the choice at the country level should also account for the health-economic objectives, the type of health infrastructure already in place as well as socio-cultural context.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on knowledge of implementation considerations.

claim: Gender-neutral strategy helps to overcome the stigma associated with a vaccine that targets only girls and aims to prevent a sexually transmitted disease.

claim: Gender-neutral vaccination provides direct health benefits in men who have sex with men.

evidence: This is based on knowledge of HPV-related diseases in men.

claim: Disease prevention programmes have been disrupted by economic sanctions.

claim: Disease prevention programmes have been disrupted by widespread vaccine hesitancy.

claim: Societal crises that disrupt disease prevention programmes are unpredictable but expected to occur.
source: Therefore, we argue that such societal crises, which are unpredictable but expected to occur, should be anticipated through careful planning of disease prevention programmes.
evidence: This is an argument based on historical patterns.

claim: EpiMetHeos was used to simulate a dynamic sexual contact network, which allows long-term and overlapping partnerships, through which HPV infections were transmitted.
source: EpiMetHeos was used to simulate a dynamic sexual contact network, which allows long-term and overlapping partnerships, through which HPV infections were transmitted.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: Atlas was used to derive the impact on cervical cancer burden based on the impact of vaccination on high-risk HPV incidence derived from EpiMetHeos.
source: Based on the impact of vaccination on high-risk HPV incidence derived from EpiMetHeos, Atlas was then used to derive the impact on cervical cancer burden.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: The models were previously calibrated to sexual behaviour, HPV prevalence, and cervical cancer incidence in India.
source: The models were previously calibrated to sexual behaviour, HPV prevalence, and/or (delete as appropriate) cervical cancer incidence in India to assess the impact of single-dose vaccination in India, while accounting for the uncertainty in the duration of vaccine protection (Man et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Man et al., 2022.

claim: A Footprinting framework was used to approximate missing data and extrapolate the impact by state in India.
source: Since the high-quality data on HPV prevalence and cervical cancer incidence data needed to calibrate the models to each Indian state were not available, we used a Footprinting framework to approximate the missing data and extrapolate the impact by state.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: EpiMetHeos was calibrated to the state of Tamil Nadu to represent the states in the high cancer incidence cluster.
source: We then calibrated EpiMetHeos to the state of Tamil Nadu to represent the states in the high cancer incidence cluster
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: EpiMetHeos was calibrated to the state of West Bengal to represent the states in the low cancer incidence cluster.
source: and the state of West Bengal to represent the states in the low cancer incidence cluster
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used in the study.

claim: Marketing authorisation has been awarded to a locally produced quadrivalent HPV vaccine in India based on successful immunobridging between the new vaccine and the existing quadrivalent vaccine (Gardasil, MSD).
source: Recently, marketing authorisation has been awarded to a locally produced quadrivalent HPV vaccine in India based on successful immunobridging between the new vaccine and the existing quadrivalent vaccine (Gardasil, MSD) (The Lancet Oncology, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to The Lancet Oncology, 2022.

claim: The model simulated vaccination with a quadrivalent vaccine targeting two high-risk types, HPV16 and HPV18, and two low-risk types, HPV6 and HPV11.
source: we simulated vaccination with a quadrivalent vaccine targeting two high-risk types, HPV16 and HPV18 (and two low-risk types, HPV6 and HPV11)
evidence: This describes the modeling assumptions.

claim: The model assumptions were based on the efficacy estimates of the IARC India vaccine trial, which considered Gardasil.
source: The efficacy estimates of the locally produced HPV vaccine were not available to us; hence, we based our model assumptions on the efficacy estimates of the IARC India vaccine trial, which considered Gardasil (Basu et al., 2021; Joshi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Basu et al., 2021 and Joshi et al., 2023.

claim: In the IARC India vaccine trial, no difference was found between the efficacy estimates of the single-dose and two-dose schedules.
source: In this trial, no difference was found between the efficacy estimates of the single-dose and two-dose schedules
evidence: This is based on trial results cited.

claim: The efficacy estimates from the IARC India vaccine trial were stable after up to 10 years' follow-up.
source: which were moreover stable after up to 10 years' follow-up
evidence: This is based on trial results cited.

claim: The model assumed 95% efficacy for HPV16 and HPV18, 9% cross-protection for HPV 31, HPV33, and HPV45, and 0% efficacy for the remaining high-risk HPV types.
source: Hence, we based the model on pooled efficacy estimates (95% efficacy for HPV16 and HPV18, 9% cross-protection for HPV 31, HPV33, and HPV45, and 0% efficacy for the remaining high-risk HPV types)
evidence: This describes the modeling assumptions.

claim: The model assumed no waning of vaccine immunity over time.
source: and assumed no waning of vaccine immunity over time
evidence: This describes the modeling assumptions.

claim: The modelled efficacy could represent vaccination under either a single-dose or two-dose schedule.
source: In doing so, the modelled efficacy could represent vaccination under either a single-dose or two-dose schedule.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling assumptions.

claim: Vaccine protection was modelled through an all-or-nothing working mechanism.
source: Vaccine protection was modelled through an all-or-nothing working mechanism, that is, if the efficacy is X%, then X% of the vaccinated individuals in the model are fully protected and 100-X% fully not protected.
evidence: This describes the modeling assumptions.

claim: Disruption was simulated to occur 10 years after the start of vaccination.
source: To assess the resilience of different vaccination strategies on cervical cancer prevention, we simulated the above scenarios first without disruption of the HPV vaccination programme, and then with disruption occurring 10 years after the start of vaccination.
evidence: This describes the modeling scenarios.

claim: The base case simulated a disruption period of 5 years with total interruption of HPV vaccine delivery (0% vaccination coverage in both boys and girls).
source: As the base case, we simulated a disruption period of 5 years with total interruption of HPV vaccine delivery, that is, 0% vaccination coverage in both boys and girls.
evidence: This describes the modeling scenarios.

claim: Sensitivity analyses considered less severe disruption with 20% and 40% vaccination coverage in girls (but still 0% in boys).
source: As sensitivity analyses, we considered less severe disruption with still 20% and 40% vaccination coverage in girls (but still 0% in boys)
evidence: This describes the modeling scenarios.

claim: Sensitivity analyses considered shorter or longer durations of disruption of 1, 2, and 10 years, and no restart of vaccination.
source: as well as shorter or longer durations of disruption of 1, 2, and 10 years, and no restart of vaccination
evidence: This describes the modeling scenarios.

claim: The mean number of cases prevented across the first 10 vaccinated birth cohorts was used to evaluate the impact prior to the disruption.
source: The mean number of cases prevented across the first 10 vaccinated birth cohorts was used to evaluate the impact prior to the disruption.
evidence: This describes the outcome measures used in the study.

claim: Resilience was defined as the mean number of cases still prevented, as a result of previous HPV vaccination, across the birth cohorts with disruption.
source: As a measure of resilience, we used the mean number of cases still prevented, as a result of previous HPV vaccination, across the birth cohorts with disruption.
evidence: This describes the outcome measures used in the study.

claim: The Segi world standard population was used for the standardisation of age-standardised incidence rates.
source: The Segi world standard population was used for the standardisation (Segi, 1960).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Segi, 1960.

claim: Model outcomes were reported as the mean and the 10th and 90th percentiles (uncertainty interval) of the simulations using the 100 parameter sets best fitting the sexual behaviour and HPV prevalence data obtained through calibration.
source: Model outcomes were reported as the mean and the 10th and 90th percentiles, that is, uncertainty interval (UI), of the simulations using the 100 parameter sets best fitting the sexual behaviour and HPV prevalence data obtained through calibration.
evidence: This describes the reporting of model results.

claim: The study did not consider the impact of screening due to the extremely low coverage of the existing screening programme in India.
source: Given the extremely low coverage of the existing screening programme in India, we have not considered the impact of screening in our study (Bruni et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bruni et al., 2022.

claim: This study adheres to HPV-FRAME, a quality framework for modelled evaluations of HPV-related cancer control.
source: This study adheres to HPV-FRAME, a quality framework for modelled evaluations of HPV-related cancer control (Reporting standard 1) (Canfell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Canfell et al., 2019.
